name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q01 - Most accurate definition of human health

questiontext.text: The term ‘Health’ is defined in many ways. The most accurate definition of the health would be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and standard medical biology, health is not merely the absence of disease or physical fitness. Rather, it represents a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being.

Step 2: Evaluation
The early humoral hypothesis considered health as a balance between bodily humors, but this concept was disproved with the discovery of blood circulation. Similarly, having a smiling face or economic prosperity can reflect emotional happiness or financial wealth, but neither provides a biologically accurate or complete measure of health.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The most accurate definition is that health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being.

answer.text: Health is the state of body and mind in a balanced condition
Health is the reflection of a smiling face
Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being
Health is the symbol of economic prosperity.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q02 - Organisms causing diseases in plants and animals

questiontext.text: The organisms which cause diseases in plants and animals are called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A wide range of organisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, and helminths cause diseases in other living organisms. Any biological entity that produces disease in a host organism is designated as a pathogen.

Step 2: Evaluation
Vectors are transmitting carriers (such as mosquitoes or ticks) that transfer an infectious agent from one host to another without being the primary cause of the disease. Insects and worms are specific taxonomic animal groups, only some of which function as disease-causing agents or vectors.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Organisms that cause disease in plants and animals are specifically called pathogens.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q03 - Clinical diagnostic test used for typhoid

questiontext.text: The clinical test that is used for diagnosis of typhoid is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Typhoid fever is a bacterial infection caused by Salmonella typhi. In clinical practice, confirmation of typhoid fever is routinely carried out by a classic serological agglutination test.

Step 2: Evaluation
The Widal test detects agglutinating serum antibodies against the lipopolysaccharide somatic (O) and flagellar (H) antigens of Salmonella typhi. In contrast, ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) is an antibody-antigen interaction assay typically used for screening conditions such as HIV, ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate) is a non-specific test for systemic inflammation, and PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is used to amplify DNA sequences.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The specific clinical test used for the diagnosis of typhoid fever is the Widal test.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q04 - Identification of infectious diseases among options

questiontext.text:
Diseases are broadly grouped into infectious and non-infectious diseases. In the list given below, identify the infectious diseases.

  1. Cancer
  2. Influenza
  3. Allergy
  4. Small pox

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Infectious (communicable) diseases are illnesses that can be transmitted from one infected individual or natural reservoir to another, caused by pathogenic biological agents such as viruses, bacteria, protozoans, or fungi. Non-infectious diseases cannot spread from person to person.

Step 2: Evaluation
Evaluating each item in the list:
• Cancer involves the uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal host cells and is non-infectious.
• Influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by the influenza virus and is highly communicable through respiratory droplets.
• Allergy is a hypersensitive immune reaction to benign environmental allergens and is non-infectious.
• Smallpox is a contagious viral illness caused by the Variola virus and is infectious.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The infectious diseases are influenza and smallpox, corresponding to statements ii and iv.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q05 - Site of formation of malarial sporozoites

questiontext.text: The sporozoites that cause infection when a female Anopheles mosquito bites a person, are formed in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The sexual phase of the life cycle of Plasmodium takes place within the female Anopheles mosquito. Gametocytes taken up during a blood meal fuse to form a motile zygote (ookinete) in the mosquito lumen.

Step 2: Evaluation
The ookinete penetrates the peritrophic membrane and epithelium of the mosquito's stomach (gut) wall to develop into an oocyst. Within this oocyst on the gut wall, asexual division known as sporogony occurs, forming thousands of infective sporozoites. Upon maturation, the oocysts burst, and the liberated sporozoites migrate through the hemolymph to the mosquito's salivary glands, where they reside until transferred into the next human host. Therefore, their site of development and formation is the gut of the mosquito.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sporozoites are formed in the gut of the mosquito.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q06 - Vector responsible for transmission of chikungunya

questiontext.text: The disease chikunguniya is transmitted by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chikungunya is a viral illness caused by an alphavirus (chikungunya virus). It is transmitted to humans through biological insect vectors that act as intermediate hosts.

Step 2: Evaluation
The primary vector responsible for the transmission of the chikungunya virus (as well as the dengue virus) is the mosquito belonging to the genus Aedes (primarily Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus). Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria, while houseflies and cockroaches function as mechanical vectors for gastrointestinal pathogens.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chikungunya is transmitted by the Aedes mosquito.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q07 - Group of symptoms indicative of pneumonia

questiontext.text: Many diseases can be diagnosed by observing the symptoms in the patient. Which group of symptoms are indicative of pneumonia?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Pneumonia is an infection of the lower respiratory tract caused by pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. The pathogen targets the alveoli of the lungs, causing them to become inflamed and filled with fluid.

Step 2: Evaluation
The accumulation of alveolar fluid leads to impaired oxygenation, causing breathing difficulties (difficulty in respiration). Other hallmark clinical features include fever, chills, cough, and headache. In contrast, constipation, abdominal pain, and stools with excess mucous and blood clots are typical of amoebiasis; nasal congestion, discharge, and sore throat are classic signs of the common cold; sustained high fever, weakness, and stomach pain characterize typhoid fever.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The group of symptoms indicative of pneumonia is difficulty in respiration, fever, chills, cough, and headache.

answer.text: Difficulty in respiration, fever, chills, cough, headache
Nasal congestion and discharge, cough, constipation, headache
High fever, weakness, stomach pain, loss of appetite and constipation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q08 - Identification of cancer causing genes in cells

questiontext.text: Cancer causing genes are called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Normal cellular genes called cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes regulate normal cellular growth and division. When these genes undergo mutations or abnormal expression, they can cause oncogenic transformation of normal cells into cancerous cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
Genes that drive malignant transformation and lead to cancer are termed oncogenes. In contrast, structural genes code for functional proteins or enzymes, regulatory genes control the transcription of other genes, and expressor genes is not a standard scientific term for cancer-inducing genetic elements.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Genes capable of causing cancer are called oncogenes.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q09 - Spread of malignant tumor cells to body

questiontext.text: In malignant tumors, the cells proliferate, grow rapidly and move to other parts of the body to form new tumors. This stage of disease is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Tumors are broadly classified as benign or malignant. Malignant tumors consist of invasive neoplastic cells that invade nearby tissue, enter the vascular or lymphatic channels, and travel to distant anatomical sites.

Step 2: Evaluation
The detachment of cells from a primary malignant tumor, their transport via blood or lymph, and their colonization of distant organs to form secondary tumors is termed metastasis. Metagenesis is the alternation of generations in invertebrate life cycles, teratogenesis refers to the production of congenital malformations in an embryo, and mitosis is regular cell division.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The process wherein cells move from a primary tumor to establish secondary tumors in other parts of the body is called metastasis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q10 - Behavioral and social maladjustment in mental health

questiontext.text: When an apparently healthy person is diagnosed as unhealthy by a psychiatrist, the reason could be that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Health is defined as a holistic state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, rather than simply the absence of physical infirmity. Mental health involves emotional balance, appropriate behavioral responses, and effective social interactions.

Step 2: Evaluation
A person who appears physically robust can still suffer from psychological, behavioral, or psychiatric disorders. A psychiatrist assesses cognitive, emotional, and social functioning; if the individual demonstrates behavioral and social maladjustment, they fail to meet the criteria for holistic health. Work productivity, economic status, or participation in sports are not diagnostic markers of mental pathology.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The person is diagnosed as unhealthy because the patient shows behavioral and social maladjustment.

answer.text: the patient was not efficient at his work
the patient shows behavioural and social maladjustment
he does not take interest in sports

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q11 - Reasons for development of rheumatoid arthritis

questiontext.text:
Which of the following are the reason(s) for Rheumatoid arthritis? Choose the correct option.

  1. The ability to differentiate pathogens or foreign molecules from self cells increases.
  2. Body attacks self cells
  3. More antibodies are produced in the body
  4. The ability to differentiate pathogens or foreign molecules from self cells is lost

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In higher vertebrates, the adaptive immune system develops self-tolerance, which is the crucial capacity to distinguish foreign antigens from self-molecules and cells. Autoimmunity occurs when self-tolerance breaks down.

Step 2: Evaluation
In autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system loses its ability to differentiate self-cells from non-self or foreign antigens. Consequently, autoantibodies and immune effector cells mount attacks against the host's own tissues, specifically damaging synovial membranes in joints. Hence, the underlying mechanisms are the loss of self/non-self discrimination and the resulting attack on self-cells. An increase in differentiation ability or general antibody production alone does not define autoimmunity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The reasons for rheumatoid arthritis are that the body attacks self-cells and the ability to differentiate foreign molecules from self-cells is lost, which corresponds to statements ii and iv.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q12 - Non mode of transmission for human immunodeficiency

questiontext.text: AIDS is caused by HIV. Among the following, which one is not a mode of transmission of HIV?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) causes Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS). Transmission of HIV strictly requires direct contact between mucosal tissue or the bloodstream and infectious bodily fluids containing the virus, such as blood, semen, vaginal fluid, or breast milk.

Step 2: Evaluation
Documented routes of HIV transmission include:
• Transfusion of contaminated blood or blood products.
• Sharing of infected hypodermic needles and syringes.
• Unprotected sexual contact with an infected individual.
• Mother-to-child transmission via placenta or lactation.
Conversely, HIV does not spread through casual social physical contact such as handshakes, hugging, touching intact skin, sharing utensils, or saliva.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Shaking hands with infected persons is not a mode of transmission of HIV.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q13 - Plant source for obtaining smack drug

questiontext.text: ‘Smack’ is a drug obtained from the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The drug commonly called ‘smack’ is chemically diacetylmorphine, an opioid narcotic. Opioids bind to specific opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract, acting as depressants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Diacetylmorphine is prepared by the acetylation of morphine. Morphine is extracted from the dried milky latex harvested from unripe seed capsules of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum. In contrast, cannabinoids are obtained from the inflorescences and leaves of Cannabis sativa, hallucinogens are extracted from Datura, and cocaine is obtained from the leaves of Erythroxylum coca.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Smack is obtained from the latex of Papaver somniferum.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q14 - Antiviral substance protecting cells from infection

questiontext.text: The substance produced by a cell in viral infection that can protect other cells from further infection is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The innate immune system includes cytokine barriers that provide early defense against viral proliferation before adaptive immune mechanisms are activated.

Step 2: Evaluation
When a host cell becomes infected by a virus, it secretes signaling glycoproteins called interferons. These interferons bind to membrane receptors on nearby healthy, uninfected cells and stimulate the synthesis of intracellular antiviral proteins, preventing further viral replication and protecting adjacent cells. Serotonin and histamine are inflammatory chemical mediators, while colostrum is the initial antibody-rich milk produced during lactation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The substance produced by virus-infected cells to protect other cells is interferon.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q15 - Immune response responsible for graft tissue rejection

questiontext.text: Transplantation of tissues/organs to save certain patients often fails due to rejection of such tissues/organs by the patient. Which type of immune response is responsible for such rejections?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Graft and organ transplantation involves the introduction of allogeneic cells possessing human leukocyte antigens (HLA) that differ from those of the recipient. The recipient's immune system identifies the transplanted tissue as non-self.

Step 2: Evaluation
The recognition of foreign histocompatibility antigens on the graft activates T-lymphocytes (specifically cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells and helper CD4+ T-cells). This activates cell-mediated immunity (CMI), which mediates direct cytotoxicity and initiates graft destruction. Although humoral antibodies may participate in certain stages of rejection, cell-mediated immunity is primarily responsible for allograft rejection.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cell-mediated immune response is responsible for the rejection of transplanted tissues and organs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q16 - Type of antibodies present in mothers colostrum

questiontext.text: Antibodies present in colostrum which protect the new born from certain diseases is of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Colostrum is the yellowish fluid produced by the maternal mammary glands during the earliest days of lactation following parturition. It imparts essential natural passive immunity to the neonate.

Step 2: Evaluation
Colostrum contains high concentrations of secretory Immunoglobulin A (\(\text{IgA}\)) antibodies. These \(\text{IgA}\) antibodies coat the mucous membranes of the infant's digestive and respiratory tracts, neutralizing pathogens before they can establish infection. In contrast, \(\text{IgG}\) is the primary isotype that traverses the placenta into fetal circulation, \(\text{IgE}\) mediates allergic reactions, and \(\text{IgD}\) acts mainly as a B-cell surface receptor.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The antibodies abundantly present in colostrum are of the \(\text{IgA}\) type.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q17 - Component stimulating adrenaline secretion from tobacco

questiontext.text: Tobacco consumption is known to stimulate secretion of adrenaline and nor-adrenaline. The component causing this could be:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Tobacco contains numerous chemical compounds, the most pharmacologically active of which are nitrogenous alkaloids that act on the autonomic nervous system.

Step 2: Evaluation
The principal alkaloid present in tobacco is nicotine. Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptors in the adrenal medulla, stimulating chromaffin cells to secrete the catecholamine hormones adrenaline and noradrenaline into systemic circulation. This hormonal release leads to an acute increase in heart rate and arterial blood pressure. Tannic acid, catechin, and curamin do not elicit this sympathomimetic response.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The component in tobacco responsible for stimulating the secretion of adrenaline and noradrenaline is nicotine.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q18 - Constituents present in antivenom against snake poison

questiontext.text: Antivenom against snake poison contains:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Passive artificial immunization involves administering pre-synthesized specific immunoglobulin molecules into an envenomated or infected individual to provide immediate neutralization of rapidly fatal toxins.

Step 2: Evaluation
Snake venom contains rapidly acting neurotoxic and hemotoxic polypeptides. The human immune system cannot produce sufficient neutralizing antibodies in time during a primary encounter. Therefore, antivenom is produced by immunizing donor animals (such as equines) with fractional doses of venom and extracting their hyperimmune serum. Antivenom thus consists of purified pre-formed antibodies that bind directly to venom antigens and neutralize them.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Antivenom against snake poison contains antibodies.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q19 - Identification of organ that is not lymphoid

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not a lymphoid tissue?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lymphoid organs and tissues are anatomical sites where lymphocytes originate, mature, and interact with antigens to mount adaptive immune responses. They comprise primary lymphoid organs (bone marrow and thymus) and secondary lymphoid organs (spleen, lymph nodes, tonsils, Peyer's patches, and mucosal lymphoid tissues).

Step 2: Evaluation
The spleen, tonsils, and thymus are all components of the lymphoid system:
• The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T-lymphocytes differentiate and mature.
• The spleen is a large secondary lymphoid organ that filters blood-borne pathogens.
• Tonsils are secondary lymphoid nodules that monitor ingested and inhaled pathogens.
In contrast, the pancreas is a dual digestive organ with exocrine acinar tissue (producing digestive enzymes) and endocrine islets of Langerhans (producing insulin and glucagon); it does not constitute a lymphoid tissue.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pancreas is not a lymphoid tissue.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q20 - Gland that reduces in size with ageing

questiontext.text: Which of the following glands is large sized at birth but reduces in size with ageing?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The thymus is a primary lobed lymphoid organ located in the superior mediastinum, anterior to the heart and deep to the sternum. It plays a central role during fetal development and childhood in conferring immunocompetence to T-lymphocytes.

Step 2: Evaluation
The thymus is large at birth and grows until puberty, after which it undergoes age-dependent involution (atrophy), shrinking in size and being progressively replaced by fat and fibrous tissue. This structural decline underlies the progressive weakening of cell-mediated immunity in elderly people. The pineal, pituitary, and thyroid glands do not undergo this dramatic atrophy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The thymus gland is large sized at birth but reduces in size with ageing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q21 - Nature and origin of toxic haemozoin

questiontext.text: Haemozoin is a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During intraerythrocytic schizogony of Plasmodium, developing trophozoites ingest hemoglobin from the cytoplasm of host red blood cells. Digestion of hemoglobin generates free heme, which is toxic to the parasite.

Step 2: Evaluation
To avoid cytotoxicity, Plasmodium biocrystallizes free heme into an insoluble, dark pigment known as haemozoin. Upon maturation, the infected red blood cells lyse and release merozoites together with haemozoin into the host bloodstream. Haemozoin acts as a pyrogen that stimulates macrophages to produce inflammatory cytokines, triggering the recurring chills and high fever characteristic of malaria. Hence, haemozoin is a toxin released specifically from Plasmodium-infected red blood cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Haemozoin is a toxin released from Plasmodium infected cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q22 - Organism not causing ringworm fungal infection

questiontext.text: Which of the following is not the causal organism for ringworm?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ringworm is one of the most common fungal infections in humans, marked by dry, scaly, pruritic lesions on skin, nails, and scalp. It is caused by keratinophilic fungi called dermatophytes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Human dermatophytosis is caused by species belonging to three recognized anamorphic genera: Microsporum, Trichophyton, and Epidermophyton. The term Macrosporum does not represent a genus of pathogenic dermatophytes causing ringworm infections.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Macrosporum is not a causal organism for ringworm.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MCQ_Q23 - Susceptibility of sickle cell anemia person to malaria

questiontext.text: A person with sickle cell anemia is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by a substitution mutation in the sixth codon of the \(\beta\)-globin gene, replacing glutamic acid with valine. Under low oxygen tension, sickle hemoglobin polymerizes, distorting erythrocytes into rigid crescent or sickle shapes.

Step 2: Evaluation
The intraerythrocytic protozoan parasite Plasmodium requires normal physiological conditions within red blood cells to survive, grow, and reproduce. In erythrocytes containing sickle hemoglobin, the parasite cannot proliferate efficiently due to potassium leakage and abnormal cell mechanics. Furthermore, infected sickle-shaped erythrocytes are rapidly filtered and destroyed by splenic macrophages before the parasites can complete schizogony. Consequently, individuals carrying the sickle mutation have an innate survival advantage against severe malaria and are significantly less susceptible to it.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A person with sickle cell anemia is less prone to malaria.
